note.text: Market incentives can encourage innovation and responsiveness, but market outcomes also have limits. An externality affects people outside the transaction. A public good is non-rival and non-excludable in the technical sense, not simply anything government owns. Unequal purchasing power can make access unequal. Monopoly power may weaken competition. Assess a market outcome by the evidence and the criterion being used, rather than assuming that private exchange always produces the best social result.

sections.heading: Understand the ideas
sections.text: Market incentives can encourage innovation and responsiveness, but market outcomes also have limits. An externality affects people outside the transaction. A public good is non-rival and non-excludable in the technical sense, not simply anything government owns. Unequal purchasing power can make access unequal. Monopoly power may weaken competition. Assess a market outcome by the evidence and the criterion being used, rather than assuming that private exchange always produces the best social result.

sections.heading: Apply the ideas locally
sections.text: Smoke from a workshop may affect neighbouring households that did not buy its product. A buyer and seller may not account for that effect in their transaction. Another example is a shared warning signal: excluding non-payers can be difficult, and one person's hearing it need not prevent others hearing it. These cases explain why a price alone may not capture every social cost or benefit.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Identify who is affected and whether they are party to the exchange. For a public-good claim, test both rivalry and exclusion. Do not call every publicly provided service a pure public good. Distinguish efficient production from fair access: they are different criteria.
